```{r, echo=FALSE}

library(pander)
```

## Introduction

Text data often contains extra spaces, has inconsistent capitalization, or combines multiple pieces of information in a single field. This tutorial demonstrates a few base R functions that make character strings easier to clean. We'll create a data frame from a small sample vector to demonstrate how each function changes the data.

```{r}

names <- c(" frodo baggins ", 
           "SAMWISE GAMGEE",
           " aragorn ",
           "legolas  greenleaf",
           " GANDALF",
           "gimli son of gloin ",
           "PEREGRIN TOOK",
           " meriadoc brandybuck",
           "ARWEN",
           " boromir "
)

names.df <- data.frame(
  original = names
)

```

Each step builds on the previous one to show how the data changes throughout the cleaning process.

## Remove Extra Spaces with `trimws()`

The `trimws()` function removes whitespace at the beginning and end of a string, but leaves spaces between words.

```{r, results='hide'}

# Remove extra spaces
names.df$trimmed <- trimws(names.df$original)

```

Compare the trimmed names to the original values below:

```{r, echo=FALSE}


pander(names.df)

```
...it's an improvement, but our data still needs some work.

## Standardize Capitalization

We can use `tolower()` to make text lowercase, `toupper()` to make it uppercase, and `tools::toTitleCase()` for title case. Combining `tolower()` and `toTitleCase()` works well when the original capitalization is inconsistent, like in our example vector.


```{r, results='hide'}

#Standardize capitalization
names.df$titlecase <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(names.df$trimmed))

```


```{r, echo=FALSE}



pander(names.df)

```

Our vector is already looking much better!

## Replace Extra Spaces with `gsub()`

The `gsub()` function searches for a pattern in a string and replaces it with something else. In our example vector, we can use it to replace multiple consecutive spaces between words with a single space. 

```{r, results='hide'}

# Replace extra spaces between words
names.df$gsub <- gsub("\\s+", " ", names.df$titlecase)

```

Compare the results after applying `gsub()` to our previously cleaned names:

```{r, echo=FALSE}


pander(names.df)

```

Now our names have consistent capitalization and spacing.

## Split Strings with `strsplit()`

The `strsplit()` function separates a string based on a specified character or pattern. For example, we can split names at spaces to separate out the first names.

`strsplit()` returns a list, so we can then use `sapply()` to extract the first element of each result.

```{r, results='hide'}


# Extract first names
names.df$first.name <- sapply(
  strsplit(names.df$gsub, " "),
  function(x) x[1])

```


```{r, echo=FALSE}

pander(names.df)

```
This allows us to extract specific information from character strings, which can be useful when working with datasets that combine multiple values in a single column.

## Conclusion

These functions provide simple ways to clean and standardize character data in R. Using `trimws()`, capitalization functions, `gsub()`, and `strsplit()` together can help prepare text data for further analysis.
